about: The five test targets of the NASA Space Apps 2026 SPHEREx challenge, with why each one is in the set. Numbers were read from Gaia DR3, AllWISE and CatWISE2020 at NASA/IPAC IRSA on 14 November 2026. Pixel shifts use the SPHEREx pixel of 6.15 arcsec. Views for every detector are in data/bands/<id>_<band>.json (and _mask.json with flagged pixels blanked).

targets.name: Barnard's Star
targets.why: Barnard's Star has the largest proper motion of any star in the sky. It is bright at every SPHEREx wavelength, so it is the cleanest first test. If the tool is right, the star walks north across a field of stars that stand still, and it lands where Gaia says it should be on each date.
targets.look_for: A bright star that steps north by a little under one pixel every six-month pass, about 2.5 pixels over the whole data set. Its core is saturated, so with the mask on it shows as a moving hole.

targets.name: Epsilon Indi B
targets.kind: pair of brown dwarfs, T1 and T6
targets.test: motion of a faint, cold source
targets.why: Epsilon Indi B is two brown dwarfs that orbit each other, and the pair orbits the bright star Epsilon Indi A. It is one of the nearest brown dwarf systems. It is faint in visible light and much brighter in the infrared, which is where SPHEREx looks. At SPHEREx resolution the two brown dwarfs are one blob, and they move less than a pixel a year, so this target tests whether the tool can show a small motion of a faint source.
targets.look_for: A faint red source in D5 that shifts by about one pixel over the data set. In a difference image it would look like a dark and bright pair, as in Backyard Worlds. Epsilon Indi A, 6.7 arcmin away, shares the same motion.
targets.note: The Gaia RUWE of 4.3 is high. A value well above 1.4 often means an unresolved pair, which is what Ba and Bb are.

targets.name: WISE 0855-0714
targets.kind: Y dwarf, the coldest known brown dwarf
targets.test: a source that only shows at long wavelengths
targets.why: WISE 0855-0714 is the coldest brown dwarf known, close to the freezing point of water, and it is the fourth nearest system to the Sun. Methane and water absorb its light on both sides of 4.6 micron, so it is invisible in visible light and close to invisible at short infrared wavelengths, but it shines near 4.6 micron. Only the longest SPHEREx detector, D6 at 4.42 to 5.00 micron, can see it. This target shows why the tool keeps each detector apart, since adding all six together would bury it.
targets.look_for: A faint source in D6 that is missing or very weak in D1 to D4, moving about 1.3 pixels a year to the west. It sits close to a field star, so the blink is the way to tell them apart.
targets.note: Too faint for Gaia. The position is from AllWISE (epoch 2010.56) and the motion from Kirkpatrick et al. 2021. In CatWISE2020 the object is split into several entries with motions near 8 arcsec per year, because it moved so far across the WISE co-adds.

targets.name: RW Aurigae
targets.why: RW Aurigae is a very young star still surrounded by gas and dust, with a companion 1.45 arcsec away. It is the prototype of its class. Dust in its disk passes in front of the star from time to time and it dims by several magnitudes, and a dimming began in 2025. It barely moves on the sky, so it tests the other half of the tool, a star that stays in place and changes.
targets.look_for: A star that stays on the same pixel while its brightness changes between passes. The two stars of the binary are one blob at SPHEREx resolution.
targets.note: Gaia lists the two stars separately. The fainter one has a RUWE of 16, so its motion is less certain.

targets.name: R Draconis
targets.kind: Mira variable, a pulsating red giant
targets.why: R Draconis is an old red giant that swells and shrinks with a period of about 246 days, and its visible brightness changes by more than six magnitudes over one cycle. The change is smaller in the infrared but still large. SPHEREx visits it about every six months, which is close to the period, so each pass catches it at a different phase. Gaia flags it as variable.
targets.look_for: A bright star that stays still and changes brightness from pass to pass. The wavelength at the star is different in each exposure, so compare passes rather than single frames.
targets.note: Distance is 1/parallax and only rough at this size of parallax. Period and V range from the AAVSO VSX catalogue.

credits: SPHEREx Level 2 images NASA/JPL-Caltech/IPAC via IRSA. Gaia DR3 ESA/Gaia/DPAC. AllWISE and CatWISE2020 NASA/JPL-Caltech, UCLA. Variable star data AAVSO VSX.
